newsitem.title: INDIA: Pakistan says Kashmir crucial to India talks.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan says Kashmir crucial to India talks.

text.p: Pakistan looks forward to resolving outstanding issues in talks with India, particularly an old dispute over the Himalayan region of Kashmir, Pakistani Foreign Secretary Shamshad Ahmad said on Thursday.

"We are absolutely clear that there is an urgent need to meaningfully address all outstanding issues, particularly the core issue of Jammu and Kashmir," Ahmad said on arrival in the Indian capital for four days of talks due to start on Friday.

Ahmad and his Indian counterpart, Salman Haidar, are to resume talks broken off three years ago mainly over the thorny issue of Kashmir, where a seven-year-old Moslem separatist movement has severely hurt ties between the neighbours.

Ahmad said: "(The) time is propitious for us to seize this opportunity for removing the root causes of tension between Pakistan and India," and added that Islamabad hoped its "sincerity of purpose" would be reciprocated by New Delhi.

In a separate statement, Haidar said: "We know that there is a great deal of expectation and we know that both sides will engage in talks in a purposeful and constructive way. Certainly that is our intention."
No agenda has been announced for the discussions, but Pakistan has repeatedly said that Kashmir is the "core issue".
The two neighbours have gone to war twice over Kashmir since independence from Britain in 1947. India controls two-thirds of the Himalayan territory and Pakistan the rest.
Jammu and Kashmir is mostly Hindu India's only Moslem-majority state.
Earlier on Thursday, Kashmiri separatist leaders demanded a role in the bilateral talks if Kashmir was to be discussed.

"The state of Jammu and Kashmir is not an integral part of India or Pakistan. Jammu and Kashmir belongs to its people. They are the principal party and should be involved in any talks on its future," Omar Farooq, chairman of Kashmir's umbrella All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, told a news conference.

The Hurriyat bands some 30 religious and political groups demanding a plebiscite in Kashmir that Pakistan, citing U.N. resolutions, has been campaigning for. India wants the dispute to be resolved bilaterally under a 1972 accord.

"The people of Jammu and Kashmir will resist any attempt at striking a deal between India and Pakistan. It will be construed as a blatant mockery of the agony of the people of Jammu and Kashmir," Farooq said.
Police and hospitals say more than 20,000 people have died since a separatist insurgency erupted in Kashmir in 1990. Islamabad denies Indian charges that it arms and trains the Moslem rebels.

Also on Thursday, about 1,000 supporters of the youth wing of India's former ruling Congress party staged a protest outside the Pakistan embassy in New Delhi against what they charged was Pakistan's support for Moslem insurgents in Kashmir.
A few protesters and some policemen were injured when police used water cannon to disperse the crowd, eyewitnesses said.
